questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 1 and is cut into 10 equal parts, so there is a mark at every tenth (0, 0.1, 0.2, ... 1). Point P sits on the 3rd mark from 0. Which number belongs to the RIGHT of P?
questions.explain: P is 3 tenths, or 0.3, so change each choice to a decimal: 35% = 0.35, which lands to the right of 0.3. The usual trap is thinking 0.25 beats 0.3 because it has more digits — check the tenths first, and 0.25 is only 2 tenths and a bit.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 1 and is cut into 10 equal parts, so there is a mark at every tenth. Which number lands strictly between the 6th mark and the 7th mark from 0?
questions.explain: The 6th and 7th marks are 0.6 and 0.7, so you need a number in between: 5/8 = 0.625. Careful — 0.59 is still less than 0.6 even though it has more digits, and 6% is only 0.06.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 1 and is divided into 20 equal parts, so each part is 0.05. Point T sits on the 9th mark from 0. Which statement about T is TRUE?
options: T lands to the left of 1/5, because 1/5 is bigger than 1/2.
T lands to the right of 1/2, because 0.45 has more digits than 0.5.
T lands between 40% and 1/2.
T lands to the right of 45%, because 45 is a much bigger number than 0.45.
questions.explain: Nine parts of 0.05 puts T at 0.45, which sits between 0.40 and 0.50. Two traps hide here: 0.45 is smaller than 0.5, and 45% IS 0.45 — the percent sign does not turn it into a big number.

questions.question: Four counters are placed on a number line that runs from 0 to 1 with a mark at every tenth. The counters sit at 0.375, at 1/9, at 0.4 and at 35%. Which counter sits furthest to the RIGHT?
questions.explain: Write them all as decimals — 0.375, 1/9 is about 0.11, 0.4, and 0.35 — so 0.4 is furthest right. Extra digits do not make a number bigger: 0.375 is less than 0.4 because 3 tenths is less than 4 tenths.

questions.question: Jamal must place one new number on the class number line, strictly between 1/2 and 3/4. Which number can he use?
questions.explain: Write the two ends as decimals, 0.5 and 0.75, then test each number: 2/3 is about 0.67, so it fits between them. Watch the traps — 0.499 is just under 0.5 even though it is long, and 0.6% means 0.006, not 0.6.

questions.question: Ana wrote four comparisons in her notebook while placing numbers on a number line. Which one is TRUE?
questions.explain: Change everything to decimals and read left to right: 3/8 = 0.375, which is right of 0.35. The others are classic traps — 0.125 is smaller than 0.2, a bigger denominator makes a unit fraction smaller, and 9% is only 0.09.

questions.question: Ms. Bhatt draws only the stretch of the number line from 0.3 to 0.5 on the board. Which number does NOT belong anywhere in that stretch?
questions.explain: As decimals the four numbers are about 0.17, then 0.4, 0.45 and 0.35, so only 1/6 falls short of 0.3. Remember that 0.45 is still less than 0.5 and 35% is just 0.35 — neither one escapes the stretch.

questions.question: At basketball practice in a Burnaby gym, four Grade 6 players track the share of free throws they made. Kai made 0.65 of his shots, Lena made 5/8 of hers, Theo made 60% of his, and Mia made 0.7 of hers. Who made the greatest share?
options: Kai, with 0.65
Lena, with 5/8
Theo, with 60%
Mia, with 0.7
questions.explain: Write every share as a decimal: 0.65, 5/8 = 0.625, 60% = 0.60, and 0.7, so Mia's 0.7 is the greatest. Extra digits do not make 0.65 beat 0.7 — 7 tenths tops 6 tenths — a bigger denominator does not make 5/8 large, and 60% is only 0.60, not sixty.

questions.question: Noah says that on the number line 0.58 sits to the right of 0.6, 'because 58 is bigger than 6'. Which reply shows Noah what is really going on?
options: He is right — 0.58 has more digits after the point than 0.6, so it is the bigger number and sits further right.
Write them as percents: 0.58 = 58%, and 58 is a much bigger number than 0.6, so 0.58 sits further right.
Write them as fractions: 0.58 = 58/100 and 0.6 = 6/10, and the bigger denominator, 100, puts 0.58 further right.
Give both the same number of places: 0.6 = 0.60, so 60 hundredths beats 58 hundredths and 0.6 is further right.
questions.explain: Give both decimals the same number of places — 0.60 against 0.58 — then compare hundredths, so 0.6 sits further right. Counting digits, or trusting the bigger denominator, will fool you every time here.

questions.question: A Grade 7 fundraising thermometer at a Victoria school runs from $0 at the bottom to $400 at the top, and a tape marker sits at the 40% line. Class 7A has raised 0.38 of the goal, 7B has raised 3/8, 7C has raised 4% and 7D has raised 0.45. Which class has passed the tape marker?
options: 7D, with 0.45 of the goal
7B, with 3/8 of the goal
7A, with 0.38 of the goal
7C, with 4% of the goal
questions.explain: The marker is at 40% = 0.40, which is $160 of the $400 goal, so compare each class with 0.40: only 0.45, or $180, is past it. Watch out — 0.38 and 3/8 = 0.375 are both under 0.40, and 4% is only 0.04.

questions.question: At a Coquitlam skate park, 7 out of every 20 skaters wore a helmet on Saturday, 32% wore one on Sunday, and 0.4 of them wore one on Monday. Ravi marks all three days on a number line from 0 to 1. Which day is furthest to the right, and why?
options: Saturday, because 0.35 has more digits than 0.4, so it must be bigger.
Monday, because 0.4 = 40%, which is right of 35% and 32%.
Sunday, because 32 is a much bigger number than 0.4 or 0.35.
Saturday, because 7/20 has a bigger denominator than 0.4 = 2/5.
questions.explain: Put all three in the same form first: 7 out of 20 = 35%, Sunday is 32%, Monday is 0.4 = 40%, so Monday sits furthest right. The percent sign does not make 32 a large number — 32% is just 0.32.

questions.question: A Vancouver Island trail is 1 km long and a marker post stands at the 60% point of the trail. Before lunch Ana had walked 0.58 km, Ben had walked 5/9 km and Cara had walked 5/8 km. Who has already passed the post?
options: Ana and Cara
Nobody has reached the post yet
Cara only
Ben and Cara
questions.explain: The post is at 60% of 1 km = 0.6 km, so compare 0.58, 5/9 (about 0.56) and 5/8 (0.625) with 0.6 — only Cara is past it. A bigger denominator does not mean a bigger fraction, so 5/9 is still short of 0.6.
